This technical and legal report provides an exhaustive analysis of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture, statutory mechanics, administrative procedures, provincial and territorial regimes, grant interactions, and judicial precedents of Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship innovation tax incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—is the federal government's largest program supporting business R&D, with published practitioner figures citing CRA program data of $4.6 billion in investment tax credits allowed across 23,677 claims processed in 2025–2026. The program delivers tax relief through a dual-benefit statutory framework. First, taxpayers may pool and deduct allowable SR&ED expenditures against business income in the current taxation year or carry them forward indefinitely under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. Second, taxpayers earn volume-based Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures under Section 127 and Section 127.1, ranging from a basic non-refundable rate of 15% to an enhanced refundable rate of 35%, which can be applied against Part I tax payable, refunded in cash, or carried back 3 years and forward 20 years.

Crucially, any technical audit or tax planning engagement in 2026 must account for the landmark legislative reforms enacted by Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (Statutes of Canada 2026, c. 3). Applying primarily to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024) and property acquired after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 enacted five structural transformations, complemented by a sixth, administrative reform introduced by the CRA:

items: Doubling the Enhanced Expenditure Limit: Increased the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000.

Broadening Phase-Out Thresholds and Introducing Revenue Elections: Expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, and introduced an elective 3-year average annual revenue phase-out alternative.

Extending Enhanced Credits to Public Companies: Extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC (up to the $6 million limit, phased out over $15 million–$75 million of 3-year average revenue) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

Restoring Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE): Reinstated SR&ED deductibility under paragraph 37(1)(b) for new or used depreciable property, and ITC eligibility under subsection 127(9) for new depreciable property, acquired after December 15, 2024 (with 40% refundability on the 35% capital ITC), alongside partial credits (25% per term over two periods, up to 50%) for Shared-Use Equipment.
Restoring Equipment Lease Costs: Reinstated eligibility for SR&ED equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024.

Launching Optional Pre-Claim Approval: Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA replaced its legacy Pre-Claim Consultation service with an optional Pre-Claim Approval regime (Form T1322), offering upfront technical eligibility certainty and cutting refundable review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: 1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Regime

Canada's federal R&D tax regime is codified within the Income Tax Act (the "Act") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations"). Unlike discretionary grant programs that depend on competitive budget envelopes, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement: any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that performs qualifying work in Canada and files the prescribed forms within the statutory reporting deadline is legally entitled to the resulting deductions and tax credits.
1.1 Subsection 248(1) — The Statutory Definition of SR&ED

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives is the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act. Conforming generally to the OECD Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of four eligible categories—paragraphs (a) through (d)—while explicitly excluding seven categories of commercial and routine activities under paragraphs (e) through (k).

cells: Requires a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis.
Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada.

Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas.

body.text: The CRA "Why" and "How" Eligibility Requirements

In its Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (published August 13, 2021), the CRA operationalizes the subsection 248(1) definition into two cumulative statutory requirements that every project must satisfy: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement.

Under the "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty), the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The focus is on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories, predictive models, or systemic know-how) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely gathering factual data or measurements. New knowledge is needed only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that whether a desired result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard professional practice. Solving a complex engineering problem using established techniques, vendor manuals, or competent professional know-how is a routine technical problem, not a technological uncertainty. Similarly, acquiring existing knowledge through staff training, hiring external consultants, or purchasing proprietary licences does not constitute technological advancement. If a team circumvents an uncertainty by adopting a workaround based on existing knowledge rather than resolving the underlying technological limitation, the work is ineligible. Conversely, integrating known components that interact in unpredictable ways can generate eligible system uncertainty if resolving the interaction requires altering the underlying subsystem technologies. Crucially, commercial failure or the rejection of a hypothesis does not disqualify a project; proving through systematic investigation why a technical hypothesis cannot work expands the technological knowledge base and satisfies the "Why" requirement.

Under the "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search), the work must be carried out through a structured, disciplined investigation by means of experiment or analysis. Following general business management protocols or trial-and-error prototyping is insufficient. A valid systematic investigation requires four sequential steps:

items: Defining the technological problem or uncertainty and establishing clear objective indicators or performance targets;

Formulating a specific hypothesis (an idea, proposed method, or causal mechanism consistent with known scientific facts) that serves as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the uncertainty;
Planning and testing the hypothesis through controlled experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively as empirical data is gathered; and
Developing logical conclusions grounded in the experimental or analytical results while maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: Distinguishing Support Work from Excluded Work

Paragraph 248(1)(d) lists eight exact categories of support work: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. None of these activities constitutes SR&ED on a standalone basis. To be claimable, support work must meet two strict statutory conditions: it must be directly in support of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada, and it must be commensurate with the needs of that eligible work.

The distinction between eligible support work under paragraph (d) and excluded work under paragraphs (e) through (k)—such as routine testing under (f) or routine data collection under (k)—turns on purpose and proportionality (commensurability). If data collection or testing is undertaken specifically to test an SR&ED hypothesis, it qualifies as support work. However, the "commensurate" standard strictly caps the claimable volume to the exact amount, size, extent, or duration necessary to validate the hypothesis. For example, if statistical engineering analysis dictates that testing 500 prototype units provides 95% statistical confidence to prove or disprove a hypothesis, but the company manufactures and tests 2,000 units, only the testing hours and materials for the first 500 units qualify as commensurate support work; the remaining 1,500 units are excluded as non-commensurate or commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i).
1.2 Section 37 — Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires two connected but legally separate computations: first, determining the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Section 37; and second, determining qualified expenditures for the Investment Tax Credit under Section 127. An expenditure can be deductible under Section 37 without generating an ITC under Section 127 (for example, non-arm's length contract payments, used capital equipment, or the 20% disallowed portion of arm's-length contracts), and conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) generates an ITC under Section 127 without ever entering the Section 37 deduction pool.

Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may deduct expenditures of a current or capital nature incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer. Rather than expiring at year-end, subsection 37(1) operates as a perpetual cumulative pool (tracked on Form T661, Part 3, Section C, Lines 420 to 470). Any undeducted balance at Line 470 carries forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in future taxation years.

cells: Pool Addition — Current Expenditures: Adds current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (salaries/wages, materials consumed/transformed, post-Dec 15, 2024 equipment leases, contract payments under subpara. 37(1)(a)(i.01), Traditional overhead, and third-party payments under subparas. 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii)).

Pool Addition — Capital Expenditures (Restored by Bill C-15): Reinstated for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) intended to be used all or substantially all (≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life, or to have ≥90% of its value consumed, in SR&ED in Canada.

Pool Addition — Assistance Repayments: Adds repayments made in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) (Form T661, Line 445).
Pool Addition — Prior Negative Pool Inclusions: Adds amounts included in the taxpayer's income in a preceding year under paragraph 12(1)(v) due to a negative Section 37 pool balance.
Pool Addition — ITC Recapture: Adds SR&ED ITC recapture amounts (and partnership recapture excess amounts) that increased Part I tax in the immediately preceding taxation year.

Pool Reduction — Assistance: Subtracts government assistance and non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures in the pool.
Pool Reduction — Super-Allowance Benefits: Subtracts provincial super-allowance benefit amounts for the year or preceding years.

Pool Reduction — Prior-Year ITCs Claimed or Refunded: Subtracts federal SR&ED ITCs deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in the preceding taxation year under subsections 127(5) and 127.1(3) (including ITCs earned on the PPA). (If this reduction drives the Section 37 pool negative at year-end, the negative balance is included in business income under paragraph 12(1)(v) or paragraph 12(1)(t)).
Pool Reduction — Prior Deductions & Insolvency: Subtracts amounts deducted in computing income in preceding years under subsection 37(1) and insolvency deductions claimed under section 61.3.

Loss Restriction Event (Acquisition of Control): Upon an acquisition of control of a corporation, a deemed year-end occurs and the unused Section 37 pool is reduced to nil unless the business to which the SR&ED related continues to be carried on for profit (or with a reasonable expectation of profit), in which case the pool is streamed and deductible only against income from that same or a similar business.

Related Corporations & Foreign SR&ED Wages: Deems SR&ED related to a business of a related corporation to relate to the claimant's business. Also permits claiming salaries/wages of employees performing SR&ED outside Canada directly in support of a Canadian project, capped at 10% of total Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages.
Available-for-Use Rule: Deems capital expenditures not to have been incurred until the depreciable property becomes available for use by the taxpayer.

Research Outside Canada: Allows a current-year income deduction for current SR&ED expenditures carried on outside Canada (other than permissible subsection 37(1.1) wages), but these expenditures do not enter the subsection 37(1) pool and earn no ITC.

Prohibition on Rights Acquisition & Priority over Donations: Subsection 37(4) prohibits any Section 37 deduction for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (preventing double-claiming of IP purchases). Subsection 37(5) mandates that an outlay qualifying as both SR&ED and a charitable gift (sections 110.1/118.1) must be claimed under Section 37.
Capital Expenditures Deemed CCA: Treats any amount deducted under subsection 37(1) in respect of paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer.

Interpretation of Canadian SR&ED Expenditures: Subparagraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) defines eligible expenditures under the Traditional Method; subparagraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) defines eligible expenditures under the Proxy Method. Paragraph 37(8)(e) (added by Bill C-15) excludes capital expenditures or rent for any building or leasehold interest therein, except a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903.

Specified Employee Restrictions: Subsection 37(9) excludes bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to specified employees. Subsection 37(9.1) caps a specified employee's deductible SR&ED salary at 5 × YMPE (prorated by days as a specified employee), while subsections 37(9.2)–(9.4) require associated corporations to share a single cap via Form T1174.

Proxy Method Election: Authorizes the taxpayer to elect on Form T661 (Line 160) to use the Proxy Method; the election must be made when the form is first filed for the year and is irrevocable for that taxation year.

Statutory Reporting Deadline: Requires Form T661 containing prescribed information to be filed within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date. Under subsection 37(12), any expenditure not reported by this deadline is statutorily deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED.

Repealed Capital Look-Through Rules: Previously required payers to strip capital elements from contract/third-party SR&ED payments; repealed by Bill C-15 for property acquired and lease costs payable on or after December 16, 2024.

body.text: 1.3 Sections 127 and 127.1 — Investment Tax Credits and Refundability Mechanics

Once allowable SR&ED expenditures are established under Section 37, Section 127 governs the calculation of qualified expenditures and the resulting Investment Tax Credit (ITC), while Section 127.1 governs cash refundability.

Under subsection 127(5), a taxpayer is permitted to deduct earned SR&ED ITCs from federal Part I tax otherwise payable. In Ainsworth Lumber Co. Ltd. v. The Queen (98-1052-IT-G, 2001), the Tax Court confirmed that because the statute uses permissive language ("may deduct"), the taxpayer may elect the order in which credits are applied. Where SR&ED is performed by a partnership, subsection 127(8) allocates the ITCs earned on partnership SR&ED expenditures to active partners at the end of the partnership's fiscal period. However, as confirmed in All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen, subsection 127(8) overrides subsection 127(10.1), meaning that SR&ED performed inside a partnership earns only the basic 15% ITC and cannot access the 35% enhanced rate, even if the partners are CCPCs. Moreover, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership must deduct 100% of its Section 37 pool in computing partnership net income in the current year and cannot carry forward a pool balance.

Subsection 127(9) establishes the core statutory definitions governing ITC calculations. The definition of "qualified expenditure" includes: (i) allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures for SR&ED directly undertaken by the taxpayer in Canada; (ii) 80% of arm's-length contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on the taxpayer's behalf in Canada and 80% of eligible third-party payments; (iii) the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under Regulation 2900(4); and (iv) 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost of First-Term or Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), while excluding prescribed expenditures (Regulation 2902), payments to non-taxable suppliers, and direct non-arm's length contract payments. Within the definition of "investment tax credit", paragraph (e) and paragraph (m) set out the basic 15% credit rate, the 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward horizon, and the mandatory 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline on Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) under paragraph 127(9)(m). Subsection 127(9) also contains the definitions of "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC), "consolidated group", and "consolidated financial statements", added by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, to bring qualifying Canadian-resident public companies into the enhanced 35% ITC regime.

Subsections 127(10.1) to (10.64) govern the enhanced 20% top-up and the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Specifically, subsection 127(10.1) adds an enhanced 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic ITC (producing a total 35% ITC) for corporations that were throughout the taxation year a CCPC or an ECPC, on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's expenditure limit. Subsections 127(10.2) (CCPC taxable capital formula), 127(10.21)–(10.4) (associated CCPC group sharing and revenue elections), 127(10.5) (short taxation year proration), and 127(10.6)–(10.64) (ECPC 3-year average revenue formula and consolidated group rules) govern the allocation and phase-out of the $6,000,000 limit.

Subsections 127(11.1)(c.1), 127(11.2), and 127(11.5)–(11.8) regulate capital and non-arm's length cost adjustments. Bill C-15 repealed paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1), which had blocked capital and lease ITCs from 2014 to December 15, 2024. Subsection 127(11.2) enforces the available-for-use timing rule. Paragraph 127(11.5)(b) sets the SUE inclusion at 1/4 (25%) of capital cost (excluding section 21 capitalized interest and subsections 13(7.1)/(7.4) adjustments). Subsections 127(11.6)–(11.8) cap the qualified expenditure when goods, services, or capital property are acquired from or leased from a non-arm's length supplier at the supplier's actual adjusted cost, stripping intercompany profit margins.

Subsections 127(18) to (20) require qualified expenditures to be reduced by government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date, with excess assistance transferable among non-arm's length group members via Form T1145. Under subsection 127(26), current expenditures (other than employee salaries/wages, which are governed by subsection 78(4)) incurred in the year but unpaid 180 days after the taxation year-end are excluded from qualified expenditures for the year and added in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid—provided the unpaid amount was reported on Form T661 within the initial 18-month reporting deadline. Subsections 127(27) to (36) trigger a clawback (addition to Part I tax payable) if property on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed (materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, or SUE) is disposed of or converted to commercial use.

Finally, Section 127.1 governs the Refundable Investment Tax Credit. Under subsections 127.1(1), (2), and (2.01), CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 100% cash refund on their 35% enhanced ITC attributable to current expenditures (and the PPA), and a 40% cash refund on their 35% enhanced ITC attributable to capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024. For a CCPC that is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) (meaning its prior-year taxable income combined with associated corporations does not exceed its "qualifying income limit"), the 15% basic ITC earned on current or capital expenditures above the expenditure limit is 40% refundable. Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5), removing it from the ITC pool and triggering the subsequent-year Section 37 pool reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) or income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(t).
1.4 Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900 to 2903)
Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations supplies the granular computational rules for SR&ED claims:

cells: Further clarifies experimental work and exclusions relating to subsection 248(1).

Traditional Method Direct Expenditures: Paragraph 2900(2)(a) covers the cost of materials consumed or transformed; paragraph 2900(2)(b) covers direct SR&ED salaries and wages; paragraph 2900(2)(c) covers other expenditures (or portions thereof) directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada that would not have been incurred had such prosecution not occurred (incremental test).

Traditional Method Premises, Facilities, and Equipment: Covers the cost of maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment used for SR&ED, plus other expenditures directly related and incremental to the provision of such premises, facilities, or equipment.
Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Rate: Sets the notional overhead proxy at 55% of the salary base (reduced from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013; fixed at 55% since 2014).
ASA Salary Rule (Proxy Method): Where an employee spends all or substantially all (≥90%) of their employment duties on SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary enters the salary base.

Overall Cap on the PPA (A − B − C): Ensures the notional PPA cannot exceed the corporation's total business deductions deducted in computing income for the year (A), minus specified deductions such as CCA, Section 37 deductions, and interest (B), and minus building rent/maintenance (C).

Specified Employee Proxy Salary Base Cap: Restricts the salary base inclusion for any specified employee to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary/wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED) for the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits), and (b) 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Year ÷ 365).

Associated Corporations Specified Employee Cap: Mandates that where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling is shared across the associated group.

Salary Base Exclusions (All Employees): Excludes from the proxy salary base for every employee: (a) taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7; (b) prior-year unpaid remuneration deemed incurred when paid under subsection 78(4) (Line 310); (c) remuneration based on profits; and (d) bonuses.

Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP): Defines properties excluded from Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), including buildings, property intended for use in assembling/constructing/commissioning a commercial manufacturing plant or line, and property intended at acquisition to be used primarily (>50%) for non-SR&ED purposes over its useful life.

Prescribed Expenditures (No ITC): Lists expenditures barred from earning an ITC under subsection 127(9), including general administration/management expenses, legal and accounting fees, patent/trademark costs, SR&ED claim preparation fees, convention/conference expenses, fines/penalties, interest and financing costs (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), and used capital property.
Prescribed Special-Purpose Buildings: Defines the narrow exception to paragraph 37(8)(e) for specialized structures approved by the Department of Finance Canada.

body.text: 2.3 Statutory Qualification Criteria for CCPCs and ECPCs
To access the enhanced 35% ITC under subsection 127(10.1), a corporate claimant must satisfy the strict statutory tests for either a CCPC or an ECPC throughout the taxation year.

Under subsection 125(7) and subsection 248(1), a corporation qualifies as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) only if it satisfies all eight statutory conditions at the end of the taxation year:

items: It is a private corporation;
It was resident in Canada and either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada continuously from June 18, 1971, to the end of the taxation year;
It is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons;
It is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation under Regulation 6700);
It is not controlled by a Canadian-resident corporation that lists its shares on a designated stock exchange outside Canada;
It is not controlled, directly or indirectly, by any combination of persons described in conditions 3, 4, and 5;

Under the hypothetical aggregation test, if all its shares owned by non-resident persons, public corporations, or foreign-listed corporations were owned by one single hypothetical person, that person would not own sufficient shares to control the corporation (Mimetex Pharmaceutical, Mindready Solutions, CO2 Solution Technologies); and
No class of its capital stock is listed on a designated stock exchange.

body.text: Introduced under subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a corporation that throughout the taxation year:

items: Is resident in Canada;
Is a "public corporation" as defined in subsection 89(1) of the Act (or would be a public corporation if the phrase "designated stock exchange in Canada" were read as "designated stock exchange");
Is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and

Would not be controlled by a single non-resident person if all shares owned by non-resident persons were owned by that particular person (eligible Canadian-resident subsidiaries of corporations meeting these four conditions also qualify as ECPCs).

body.text: 2.4 Mathematical Formulas for the $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Outs
CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, unless a CCPC elects to use the revenue method under subsection 127(10.31) or (10.32), its annual expenditure limit is determined solely by its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across all associated corporations under subsection 127(10.21)). Note that prior-year taxable income no longer reduces the federal CCPC expenditure limit, though it still governs the Qualifying Income Limit under subsection 127.1(2) and the Ontario OITC limit:

In this formula, variable A is $0 if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and its associated corporations) is $15,000,000 or less, and in any other case equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. Algebraically, because the ratio of $6,000,000 to $60,000,000 is 0.10, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000 (10% of the excess), reaching zero at $75,000,000:
ECPC and Elective CCPC Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Subsections 127(10.6), (10.31), and (10.32))

For an ECPC, the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6) uses the exact same linear phase-out formula, except that variable A is measured by the excess over $15,000,000 (up to $60,000,000, eliminating the limit at $75,000,000) of the corporation's average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years. If the ECPC has fewer than 3 preceding fiscal years, subsection 127(10.64) mandates that average annual revenue is calculated over the actual number of preceding fiscal years (1 or 2 years). If the ECPC is a member of a "consolidated group", subsection 127(10.62) requires annual revenue to be determined from the group's consolidated financial statements (as defined in subsections 233.8(1) and 127(9)), and the group must share a single expenditure limit. Under subsection 127(10.31) (single CCPC) and subsection 127(10.32) (associated CCPC group), a CCPC with high balance-sheet debt or equity (high taxable capital) but low revenue (such as a pre-revenue biotechnology or hardware firm) may elect on its prescribed form to have its expenditure limit determined using the 3-year average annual revenue formula instead of taxable capital. When calculating associated group revenue, the group must include each corporation's reasonable share of partnership or trust revenue and may make reasonable adjustments to eliminate intercompany revenues as a single economic entity.
Qualifying Income Limit (QIL) Formula (Subsection 127.1(2))

For a CCPC spending above its $6 million expenditure limit, the basic 15% ITC earned on excess expenditures is 40% refundable only if the CCPC is a "qualifying corporation"—meaning its prior-year taxable income (combined with associated corporations) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit (QIL). Associated Corporations and Short Taxation Years

Under subsections 127(10.21), (10.3), and (10.4), associated CCPCs must share a single expenditure limit and file an allocation agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Ignoring association rules under section 256 is a frequent audit failure; if the group fails to file Schedule 49 after a CRA demand, the Minister allocates the limit under subsection 127(10.4). Furthermore, under subsection 127(10.5), if a taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks, the corporation's expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the otherwise determined limit by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365. For example, a CCPC with a full $6,000,000 baseline limit that experiences a 273-day short taxation year has a prorated expenditure limit of $6,000,000 × (273 ÷ 365) = $4,487,671.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Cost Rules
3.1 Salaries and Wages (Form T661, Part 3, Lines 300 to 315)

Salaries and wages typically represent the largest component of a Canadian SR&ED claim and are governed by the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), subsection 248(1), section 37, and Regulation 2900.
Eligible vs. Ineligible Remuneration

Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (i.e., sections 5 to 8 T4 employment income), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Eligible wage components incurred for SR&ED include regular base salary and hourly wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, commissions, tips, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, inducement or non-competition payments, cash taxable benefits, and qualifying non-cash taxable benefits under section 6 (provided the benefit reflects a reasonable estimate of actual employer cost, excludes GST/HST/PST where an Input Tax Credit is claimed per subsection 248(16), and is not double-claimed as a regular business expense). Bonuses and remuneration based on profits are eligible SR&ED wages under Section 37 only for non-specified employees (though excluded from the proxy salary base for all employees under Regulation 2900(9)).
Conversely, four categories of compensation are strictly ineligible as SR&ED salaries and wages:

items: Dividends: Dividends paid to founder-shareholders are a distribution of after-tax corporate profits on share capital, not income from employment. Founders who compensate themselves via T5 dividends rather than T4 payroll generate $0 in claimable SR&ED wages or proxy overhead, regardless of how many hours of hands-on R&D they perform.

Stock Option Benefits (Section 7): Explicitly excluded from SR&ED expenditures for taxation years after November 14, 2005 (following legislative amendments overriding Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149).

Employer Payroll Taxes and Related Benefits (Under Proxy Method): Employer contributions to CPP/QPP, EI, EHT, provincial workers' compensation (WSIB/CNESST), and group health or dental plans are not "salary or wages" of the employee; they cannot be claimed on Lines 300/305 and are absorbed within the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method (though claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method).

Unpaid Remuneration (180-Day Rule under Subsection 78(4)): Any salary, wage, or bonus accrued at year-end that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed under subsection 78(4) not to have been incurred in that year. It must be reported as unpaid on Line 315 of Form T661. When actually paid in a subsequent year, it is claimed on Line 310 as a current SR&ED expenditure for that later year, but under Regulation 2900(9) it is permanently excluded from the proxy salary base.

body.text: Directly Engaged Tasks vs. Supervision and the ASA (90%) Rule

Eligibility of an employee's wages depends on actual tasks performed, never on job title. Directly engaged hands-on work includes preparing equipment or materials for experiments, executing tests or analyses, writing experimental code, building non-commercial prototypes, and recording experimental data. Non-specialized shop-floor operators feeding raw materials into an experimental machine qualify if directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Managers and executives qualify only for the portion of time spent providing direct technical input, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects (assigning technical personnel, setting experimental priorities, developing technological strategies), or directing the ongoing course of experiments. Work beyond first-line technical supervision—such as general corporate management, budgeting, commercial feasibility studies, patent or licensing administration, human resources, or sales—does not qualify.

Under the All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Rule (Regulation 2900(5)), if an employee spends 90% or more of their total employment time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary and wages is treated as directly engaged in SR&ED. If they spend less than 90% of their time on SR&ED, only the exact substantiated percentage of time spent on SR&ED may be claimed. Furthermore, under subsections 37(1.1) and 37(1.5) (Lines 307 and 309), where an employee of the claimant performs SR&ED work physically outside Canada that is integral to and directly supports an SR&ED project carried on in Canada, those wages are deemed incurred in Canada up to a maximum ceiling of 10% of the claimant's total Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages (Lines 300 + 305).
Specified Employees and YMPE Caps (2024–2026)

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who either: (a) is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time during the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or any related corporation; or (b) does not deal at arm's length with the employer (e.g., a spouse, child, sibling, or controlling individual under section 251). Under the constructive ownership rules of subsection 248(1), shares held by a non-arm's length person count toward the employee's 10% threshold, and a beneficiary of a discretionary family trust is deemed to own 100% of the shares held by the trust.
Specified employees are subject to four strict statutory restrictions:

items: No Bonuses or Profit-Based Pay (Subsection 37(9)): All bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to a specified employee are completely disallowed.

Direct SR&ED Wage Cap — 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1), Line 305): The maximum direct SR&ED salary claimable for a specified employee in a taxation year cannot exceed 5 × YMPE × (Days as Specified Employee in Year ÷ 365), where YMPE is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends.

Proxy Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Total Wage or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7), Part 5 Lines 850–858): When computing the salary base for the 55% PPA, a specified employee's inclusion is capped at the lesser of: (i) their direct SR&ED salary (Line 305 + Line 309); (ii) 75% of their total annual salary/wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses/benefits); and (iii) 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Year ÷ 365).

Mandatory Associated Corporation Allocation (Subsections 37(9.2)–(9.4) & Regulation 2900(8)): If a specified employee receives salary from two or more associated corporations, the 5 × YMPE direct wage cap and 2.5 × YMPE proxy cap must be shared across the group via Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED). If the associated corporations fail to file the agreement, none of the specified employee's salary is claimable by any corporation in the group.

body.text: 3.2 Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must choose annually between two mutually exclusive overhead calculation methods on Form T661: the Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 and completing Part 5) or the Traditional Method (elected by ticking Line 162 and claiming actual overhead on Line 360). Under subsection 37(10), the election is made on the day Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is strictly irrevocable for that year, though a taxpayer may switch methods from one taxation year to the next. If no box is ticked, the Traditional Method applies by default.
Note on the Prescribed Proxy Rate (55% vs. Outdated 65% Claims)

A recurring compliance error in secondary literature and automated summaries is the assertion that the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is 65% of direct salaries. This is statutorily incorrect. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA rate was 65% for taxation years ending before 2013, 60% prorated for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% of the eligible salary base since January 1, 2014. Using 65% overstates the notional overhead by 10 percentage points and triggers immediate reassessment.
Mechanics of the Proxy Method (PPA)

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead or support staff costs on Line 360. Instead, the actual overhead expenses incurred by the business (utilities, office supplies, clerical support wages, employer CPP/EI/benefits, maintenance) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Act, rather than entering the Section 37 SR&ED pool. In Part 5 of Form T661, the claimant computes the salary base (Line 818) by summing the directly engaged SR&ED salaries of non-specified employees (Lines 300 + 307, less bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and Line 310 prior-year unpaid wages per Regulation 2900(9)) and the capped proxy salaries of specified employees (Line 816, subject to the 75% and 2.5 × YMPE limits per Regulation 2900(7)). The claimant multiplies the salary base (Line 818) by 55% at Line 820 to determine the PPA, and transfers the PPA to Line 502 in Part 4.

Under Regulation 2900(6), the PPA transferred to Line 502 cannot exceed the overall cap calculated by the formula A − B − C, where A is total business deductions claimed in computing net income for tax purposes, B is specifically excluded deductions (CCA, Section 37 SR&ED deduction on Schedule 1 Line 411, interest, bad debts, etc.), and C is building rent and maintenance expenses. Because the PPA is a notional addition to qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9), it earns federal and provincial ITCs at the full applicable rate (e.g., 35% federal refundable ITC for a CCPC/ECPC), even though it is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool.
Mechanics of the Traditional Method (Regulation 2900(2)(c) & 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is calculated (Line 502 is $0). Instead, the claimant identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360, which are added to both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022) and Regulation 2900(2)(c), every overhead item claimed on Line 360 must pass a strict two-part cumulative test:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to one of three elements: (a) the SR&ED work itself; (b) the SR&ED staff; or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to prosecute SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed costs that do not vary with SR&ED activity fail the incremental test.

body.text: 3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026) and Regulation 2900(2)(a), the cost of materials may be claimed only in the taxation year in which the materials are physically consumed (Line 320) or transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—never when merely purchased or held in inventory. To constitute "materials for SR&ED", the item must be a physical, tangible substance (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process composes the body of a thing on which the SR&ED is performed.

Claimable cost represents the laid-down cost, including invoice price, customs and excise duties, transportation, and storage costs. If the claimant uses self-manufactured inventory in SR&ED, the claimable material cost includes raw materials, direct production labour, and the allocable share of manufacturing overhead under both the Proxy and Traditional methods. If purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) caps the qualified expenditure at the supplier's cost (excluding profit). Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless with no residual commercial value as a result of the SR&ED (e.g., galvanized metal parts destroyed in stress testing, ink and cardboard boxes discarded after experimental printing runs, or seeds, agar, fungal media, and fertilizers applied to experimental test plots). Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials or components incorporated into a tangible object resulting from SR&ED that retains value—such as a custom product, a commercial asset, or experimental production that is later sold or used commercially. Conversely, items used during SR&ED that do not compose the physical body of the experimental object—such as petri dishes, beakers, test tubes, pipettes, flasks, filter papers, microscopes, cleaning products, acids, solvents, lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and general facility electricity or heating—are not materials for SR&ED. Under the Proxy Method they are covered by the 55% PPA; under the Traditional Method they may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead.
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to (36))

When property on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed—specifically materials transformed (Line 325), ASA capital equipment (Line 390), or Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504)—is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (36) claw back the credit by adding the recaptured amount directly to federal Part I tax payable. For materials transformed or ASA capital property, the recapture equals the lesser of: (a) the ITC originally earned on the property/materials, or (b) the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value of the property at the time of commercial conversion.

A critical planning distinction applies between purchased and self-manufactured components. As illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 to manufacture a custom part used as a material transformed in an experimental prototype and later converts the prototype to commercial use, the full $12,000 purchase price is subject to ITC recapture. Conversely, if the claimant manufactures that exact same part in-house using its own employees and raw materials, there is no ITC recapture on the in-house SR&ED salaries or overhead—recapture applies solely to the raw material cost.
3.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments
Arm's-Length SR&ED Subcontractors (Form T661, Line 340)

When a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract payment enters the Section 37 deduction pool at Line 340 (under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)). However, since January 1, 2013, subsection 127(9) restricts the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to 80% of the eligible contract amount (subtracting 20% at Line 529 in Part 4). The SR&ED work must be physically performed in Canada; payments to foreign contractors performing R&D outside Canada are deductible under subsection 37(2) but earn 0% ITC. Furthermore, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" under subsection 127(9)—defined as a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident carrying on business through a Canadian permanent establishment.

A payer can contract out standalone support work (such as testing, CAD design, or computer programming under paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's-length Canadian contractor, provided that support work is commensurate with and directly supports the payer's own eligible Canadian SR&ED project. The contractor performing pure support work cannot claim SR&ED on its own return because support work alone is not SR&ED, and even if the contractor performs full SR&ED, the payer's payment is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(18) that reduces the contractor's qualified expenditures to prevent double-dipping. If an arm's-length contract invoice is unpaid 180 days after year-end (subsection 127(26)), Part 4 of Form T661 first removes 20% on Line 529 and then deducts the remaining 80% as an unpaid amount on Line 520; when paid in a subsequent year, 80% of the paid amount is added back on Line 500.
Non-Arm's Length (NAL) Contracts (Line 345 & Form T1146)

Under subsection 127(9), payments made to a person or partnership with whom the claimant does not deal at arm's length (Line 345) for performing SR&ED do not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer. Instead, the NAL performer calculates its own qualified expenditures and may transfer those qualified expenditures to the NAL payer by filing a joint agreement on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), reported at Line 508 (transferee) and Line 540 (transferor) of Form T661.
Third-Party Payments (Line 370, Form T1263)

Unlike a subcontractor agreement where the payer controls the specifications and owns exclusive IP, a third-party payment (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii); CRA Third-Party Payments Policy, updated March 30, 2022) is a payment in money or in kind (valued at fair market value) made to an eligible entity to be used for basic research, applied research, or experimental development in Canada related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Like arm's-length contracts, 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for the ITC (20% deducted at Line 529), and claimants must attach Form T1263 (or Schedule A) for each payment.

body.text: 3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most consequential reforms enacted by Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the restoration of SR&ED tax incentives for capital property and equipment leases acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024. Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED. For property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) establish three distinct regimes.
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The ASA (≥90%) Intent Test (Line 390)

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 (and reported on Lines 262–263 of Part 2 and Part 6B, Box 780) if, at the time of acquisition (when available for use under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2)), the claimant intended that the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or that all or substantially all (≥90%) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (e.g., experimental tooling, moulds, or pilot rigs rendered valueless by testing).

When this intent test is satisfied, 100% of the capital cost enters the Section 37 pool (Line 390), allowing an immediate 100% write-off against income (deemed to be CCA under subsection 37(6), so the asset must not be included on T2 Schedule 8). For ITC purposes, 100% of the cost of new ASA equipment enters the qualified expenditure pool, earning a 35% ITC (for CCPCs/ECPCs within the $6M limit) that is 40% refundable in cash (or 15% above the limit / for large firms). Land (non-depreciable), buildings and leasehold interests in buildings (excluded by paragraph 37(8)(e), except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903), inventory, and goodwill are strictly excluded. Used depreciable property meeting the ASA test can be deducted 100% under Section 37 on Line 390, but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 and must be subtracted on Line 532 in Part 4 so that it earns 0% ITC.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — The Primarily (>50% to <90%) Actual Use Test (Line 504)

Often a manufacturer or hardware studio acquires new machinery after December 15, 2024 (e.g., a CNC machine, 3D printer, or high-performance test bench) that is used partly for SR&ED and partly for commercial production, failing the ≥90% ASA lifetime intent test. Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 127(11.5)(b), the equipment qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 (and Part 6C, Box 788) if it meets six conditions:

items: It is depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024;
It is brand-new property (never used, acquired for use, or rented for any purpose before acquisition);
It does not meet the ≥90% ASA capital expenditure test;

It is not a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (i.e., not a building, not intended for commissioning a commercial plant or line, and not intended at acquisition to be used primarily [>50%] for non-SR&ED over its total useful life);

It is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, and phones are excluded; however, computers, hardware, software, and ancillary computing equipment are NOT GPOEF and can qualify as SUE); and

It is actually used primarily (>50% but <90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (from the date available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later) and/or the Second Period (from the date available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months later).

body.text: SUE capital costs never enter the Section 37 deduction pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the equipment under normal Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes on T2 Schedule 8. For ITC purposes on Line 504, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money interest under s. 21) is deemed a qualified expenditure at the end of the First Period (First-Term SUE), and a second 1/4 (25%) is deemed a qualified expenditure at the end of the Second Period (Second-Term SUE)—yielding an ITC on up to 50% of the equipment's capital cost. If SUE is later sold or converted to commercial use, subsection 127(27)(d) caps ITC recapture at the lesser of the SUE ITC earned or the ITC rate applied to 25% (if only First-Term claimed) or 50% (if both terms claimed) of the proceeds of disposition.

To illustrate the SUE timeline rules, Section 3.5 of the CRA SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy provides the following example: a corporation with a December 31 year-end buys a new machine for $300,000 on January 2, 2025 (intending 75% SR&ED use over its life, so it is not a PDP). In the 2025 tax year (Jan 2 – Dec 31, 2025), the machine runs 1,600 hours (1,300 SR&ED / 300 commercial); because the period from January 2, 2025 to December 31, 2025 is less than 12 full months, no SUE claim is made in 2025 and only regular Schedule 8 CCA is claimed. In the 2026 tax year (First Period ends Dec 31, 2026 — at least 12 months), the machine runs 2,000 hours (1,600 SR&ED / 400 commercial); cumulative First Period operating time (Jan 2, 2025 – Dec 31, 2026) is 3,600 hours, of which 2,900 hours (81%) were SR&ED, qualifying the machine as First-Term SUE in 2026 and adding 25% × $300,000 = $75,000 to Line 504. In the 2027 tax year (Second Period ends Dec 31, 2027 — at least 24 months), the machine runs 2,000 hours (800 SR&ED / 1,200 commercial); cumulative Second Period operating time (Jan 2, 2025 – Dec 31, 2027) is 5,600 hours, of which 3,700 hours (66%) were SR&ED. Even though 2027 standalone SR&ED use was only 40% (800/2,000), cumulative Second Period use exceeded 50% (66%), so it qualifies as Second-Term SUE in 2027, adding another $75,000 to Line 504.
3. Equipment Lease Costs (Lines 350 & 355 — Post-December 15, 2024)
For equipment lease payments that first become payable after December 15, 2024 (reported on Part 6A, Box 759):

items: ASA Use (≥90% of operating time in the full tax year): 100% of the lease cost is claimable on Line 350 under both the Traditional and Proxy methods (except that GPOEF lease costs cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method).

Primarily Use (>50% to <90% of operating time in the full tax year): Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) is claimable on Line 355 (if used ≤50%, $0 is claimable under Proxy). Under the Traditional Method, the exact proportional percentage of SR&ED usage (even if ≤50%, provided it is directly related and incremental) is claimable as overhead on Line 360.

body.text: 4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes & Stacking Mechanics

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack atop the federal SR&ED program (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not operate standalone territorial/provincial R&D tax credits). Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" that reduces the federal Section 37 deduction pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (unless the taxpayer validly renounces or waives a provincial credit by its statutory deadline). Conversely, the federal SR&ED ITC never reduces the calculation base of any provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.

1. Ontario: Compound Phase-Out Mechanics and Triple-Credit Stacking (OITC + ORDTC + Federal SR&ED)

Ontario did not raise its $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit when the federal limit doubled to $6,000,000. However, Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement confirmed that 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) are restored to both the OITC and ORDTC bases (whereas pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40% for OITC).

On Schedule 566, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit under subsection 96(3.1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) is subject to two independent prior-year grinds across the associated group—prior-year federal taxable income ($500,000 to $800,000) and prior-year specified capital/taxable capital employed in Canada ($25,000,000 to $50,000,000)—which compound multiplicatively rather than merely taking the lesser of the two:
OITC Expenditure Limit = ($8,000,000 − 10 × max($500,000, Prior-Year Taxable Income)) × ($25,000,000 − max(0, Prior-Year Taxable Capital − $25,000,000)) ÷ $25,000,000

To verify the compound grind, if an Ontario scale-up has $700,000 in prior-year taxable income and $30,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, the taxable income component reduces the base limit from $3,000,000 to $8,000,000 − 10($700,000) = $1,000,000. The taxable capital component leaves a surviving fraction of ($25M − $5M) ÷ $25M = 80%. Multiplying the two yields an OITC expenditure limit of $1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000 (generating a maximum 8% OITC of $64,000)—whereas erroneously taking the lesser of the two tests would have overstated the limit at $1,000,000.

Because OITC is treated as government assistance that reduces the ORDTC base, and both OITC and ORDTC reduce the federal SR&ED base, the statutory calculation sequence for a qualifying CCPC with $1,000,000 of eligible current Ontario SR&ED expenditures (under all phase-out thresholds) is:

items: Step 1 — Calculate 8% Refundable OITC (Schedule 566): $1,000,000 × 8% = $80,000 (cash refund).

Step 2 — Calculate 3.5% Non-Refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508): Reduce the $1,000,000 Ontario base by the $80,000 OITC to get $920,000; apply 3.5% × $920,000 = $32,200 (non-refundable Ontario tax offset; combined Ontario recovery = $112,200 or 11.22%).

Step 3 — Reduce Federal Qualified Expenditure Pool (Form T661, Line 513/514): Subtract both Ontario credits (unless ORDTC is waived/renounced) from the federal base: $1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200 = $887,800.
Step 4 — Calculate 35% Federal Refundable ITC (Schedule 31): $887,800 × 35% = $310,730 (cash refund).

Step 5 — Total Combined Recovery: $80,000 (OITC) + $32,200 (ORDTC) + $310,730 (Federal ITC) = $422,930 (42.29% of spend, comprising $390,730 [39.07%] in immediate cash refunds and $32,200 [3.22%] in non-refundable Ontario tax credits). (If the CCPC is in a tax loss position and waives/renounces the non-refundable $32,200 ORDTC under subsection 96(14) or the ORDTC waiver provision on or before its T2 filing-due date, the federal base remains $1,000,000 − $80,000 = $920,000, increasing the 35% federal cash refund to $322,000 and total immediate cash to $402,000 [40.20%]).

body.text: 2. Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Consolidation & Pre-Commercialization Expansion)

In the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget (detailed in Revenu Québec Tax News of July 9, 2025), the Québec government enacted a comprehensive reform of provincial innovation taxation by creating the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation), applicable to taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated seven legacy measures: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages of R&D Researchers (Form RD-1029.7-V); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centres (Form RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V); (4) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V); (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credit (retaining only fashion design); and (7) the individual income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. Publication IN-109-V has been officially cancelled by Revenu Québec, and individuals can no longer claim R&D credits for years beginning after March 25, 2025, as CRIC is restricted to qualified corporations and corporate members of qualified partnerships.

The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit at an increased rate of 30% on up to $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold—regardless of the corporation's total asset size—and a 20% refundable basic rate on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 band. Associated corporations share the $1,000,000 limit using Form RD-1029.8.EN-T. For each taxation year, the corporation's reducible expenditures must first exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold.

In addition to Québec R&D salaries, subcontractor payments, and research organization payments (claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T alongside Form RD-222-V), the CRIC expands eligibility to: (1) pre-commercialization activities (reported on Form RD-1029.8.PR-T), including technological validations, testing, studies to satisfy regulatory certification requirements, and product design, provided they are a continuation of R&D undertaken in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation; and (2) capital expenditures for acquiring depreciable property used for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Québec nexus ratio for the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) is computed using R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (without reduction by the CRIC exclusion threshold, and excluding pre-commercialization expenditures). Software firms in Québec may also evaluate the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE / CDAEIA, Form CO-1029.8.36.DA), which incorporates an AI integration requirement, exclusion threshold, and sliding-scale rates up to 30%.
3. British Columbia: Bill 2 (2026) Permanence and Full Federal Harmonization

Prior to 2026, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit (Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.), Form T666) was subject to a statutory sunset date of September 1, 2027 and a $3,000,000 refundable cap. Under Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the B.C. legislature made the 10% B.C. SR&ED tax credit permanent and harmonized B.C.'s parameters with federal Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Specifically, the 10% refundable B.C. credit expenditure limit doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual B.C. cash refund from $300,000 to $600,000); eligibility for the 10% refundable credit was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs; the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range expanded to $15,000,000–$75,000,000; and capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 were restored as B.C. qualified expenditures.
5. Interaction with Direct Government Grants, Assistance, and Stacking Rules

Canadian technology, life sciences, and manufacturing enterprises routinely stack federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits with direct non-dilutive government grants and contributions. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18), "government assistance" (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, and provincial tax credits from any municipal, provincial, federal, or foreign public authority) and "non-government assistance" (inducements or reimbursements included under paragraph 12(1)(x)) reduce both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool on a project-by-project basis in the taxation year in which the assistance is received, entitled to be received, or can reasonably be expected to be received on or before the filing-due date.
5.1 Major Federal Innovation Funding Programs and SR&ED Interaction

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's primary direct R&D grant program for incorporated SMEs (500 or fewer employees), with practitioner analyses citing $562 million in total program spend ($437 million in grants) across roughly 3,360 funded firms in FY2024–2025. Managed through regional Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), IRAP provides monthly non-repayable reimbursements covering up to 80% of eligible internal R&D technical salaries and up to 50% of Canadian subcontractor costs (with a reported median award of $75,000, typical multi-year awards of $75,000–$1,000,000, and a $10,000,000 ceiling for major projects). IRAP requires pre-approval before eligible expenses are incurred.

For larger industrial projects, the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) supports large-scale R&D, commercialization, and clean technology scale-up projects (typically requiring minimum project costs of $10,000,000+). SIF contributions—including both unconditional grants and forgivable loans lacking firm commercial repayment terms—constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9). In CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57), the courts confirmed that government R&D loans related to SR&ED reduce the SR&ED expenditure pool. Under NSERC Alliance Grants and CIHR Partnerships, funds flow to the academic institution rather than the corporate sponsor, so the corporation claims SR&ED (as a third-party payment at 80% inclusion on Line 370) strictly on its own direct cash and in-kind contribution to the university. Finally, the Clean Technology Investment Tax Credits enacted in Bill C-59 (Royal Assent June 20, 2024) apply to commercial capital asset acquisitions, whereas SR&ED applies to R&D labour, materials, overhead, and dedicated R&D capital equipment—allowing clean-tech developers to claim SR&ED on experimental development and Clean Tech ITCs on commercial deployment assets in the same year, provided the same capital asset is not double-claimed.
5.2 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) + NRC IRAP Stacking Leverage Mechanic

A critical statutory feature of the Canadian SR&ED regime is the interaction between NRC IRAP wage subsidies and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method. On Form T661, the salary base in Part 5 (Lines 810–818) is computed directly from the gross eligible SR&ED salaries reported on Lines 300 and 305 in Part 3—before subtracting government assistance. Government assistance (such as an 80% IRAP salary reimbursement) is subtracted only later in Part 3, Section C (reducing the Section 37 deduction pool) and in Part 4 (Line 515, reducing the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool). Consequently, an IRAP grant does NOT reduce the salary base used to compute the 55% PPA; the claimant earns the full 55% notional overhead proxy on 100% of its eligible SR&ED salaries, even if IRAP reimbursed 80% of those salaries.
Worked Numerical Proof of IRAP + SR&ED Proxy Stacking

Suppose an Ontario-based qualifying CCPC incurs $250,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries (non-specified employees) and $50,000 in consumed materials ($300,000 total R&D spend), elects the Proxy Method, and receives an NRC IRAP grant covering 80% of the salaries ($200,000):

items: Gross Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Part 3, Line 380): $250,000 (Line 300 Salaries) + $50,000 (Line 320 Materials) = $300,000.
Prescribed Proxy Amount Calculation (Part 5, Line 820 to Line 502): The salary base at Line 818 is the full $250,000 gross SR&ED salary (unreduced by IRAP). Thus, PPA = 55% × $250,000 = $137,500.
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance (Part 4, Line 511): $300,000 (Allowable Spend) + $137,500 (PPA) = $437,500.
Deduction of IRAP Government Assistance (Line 515): Subtract the $200,000 IRAP grant: $437,500 − $200,000 = $237,500 net qualified expenditures (prior to provincial credit grinds).

Ontario OITC (8%) and Federal ITC (35%) Calculation: The 8% Ontario OITC on $237,500 equals $19,000 (cash refund). Subtracting the $19,000 OITC leaves a federal qualified expenditure base of $237,500 − $19,000 = $218,500, which at the 35% federal enhanced rate generates $76,475 in federal cash refund.

Total Non-Dilutive Cash Recovery: Combining $200,000 (IRAP) + $19,000 (OITC) + $76,475 (Federal SR&ED) yields $295,475 on $300,000 of actual cash outlay (98.49% combined cost recovery, leaving a net out-of-pocket cost of $4,525, subject to applicable grant agreement stacking caps, which typically limit direct grant assistance to 75% of eligible project costs).

body.text: Treatment of Provincial Assistance Attributable to the PPA

Under Section 4.5 of the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a claimant uses the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as the 8% Ontario OITC) that was earned on the notional PPA does not reduce the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d), because the PPA was never in the Section 37 pool. Instead, the PPA portion of the provincial credit is included directly in the corporation's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) on T2 Schedule 1 in the year received. However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, 100% of the provincial R&D credit (both the current expenditure portion and the PPA portion) reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(18).
6. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Form T661 (Version 26), Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Administration
6.1 Governing Authorities and Administrative Division of Labour

Canada's R&D tax system operates under a dual federal institutional structure. The Department of Finance Canada formulates tax policy, drafts statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (such as Bill C-15), and approves prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program and all harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (except Québec and Alberta). Within the CRA's SR&ED Directorate and Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), technical eligibility is evaluated by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), while expenditure verification, salary caps, overhead allocations, and assistance grinds are audited by Financial Reviewers (FRs). Revenu Québec and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance independently administer the Québec CRIC (alongside the Ministère des Finances du Québec and Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie) and the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), respectively.
6.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations (T2 Return): Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, adding 12 months yields an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the taxation year-end. A corporation should file its T2 return within 6 months and may submit or amend its Form T661 and Schedule 31 at any time up to the 18-month deadline.

Individuals / Sole Proprietors (T1 Return): Because a business individual's T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following calendar year (5.5 months after December 31), adding 12 months yields a reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the taxation year-end.

Partnerships (T5013 Return): Form T661 must be filed by the partnership with its T5013 Partnership Information Return no later than 12 months after the earliest filing-due date of any member (partner) for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ended.

body.text: Following legislative amendments effective November 17, 2005 (which overrode Alex Parallel Computers Research Inc. v. Canada, T-1512-97), the CRA and the Minister of National Revenue have no statutory authority or taxpayer relief discretion to extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for any reason. If Form T661 or Schedule 31 is filed past the 18-month deadline, or if a specific expenditure line item or unpaid amount is omitted at the 18-month mark, subsection 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) permanently bar the deduction and the ITC (Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211; Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9).
6.3 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval regime using Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval), replacing the discontinued Pre-Claim Consultation service. Pre-Claim Approval enables businesses to obtain an upfront evaluation of their planned or recently initiated R&D work to confirm it satisfies SR&ED requirements before incurring significant project costs or filing a tax return.
To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business and project must satisfy five mandatory criteria:

items: The applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership;
The business must have gross business income of less than $25,000,000;
The business must be in good standing with the CRA;
The proposed project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim; and
The project must not involve issues currently under litigation.

body.text: To apply, the business requests a Pre-Claim Approval case number, completes Form T1322 detailing the project and supporting documentation, and uploads the application via My Business Account. Published practitioner guides note an 8-week determination target and state that the CRA can approve projects for up to 3 years. Pre-Claim Approval determines technical project eligibility only; it does not audit expenditure quantum and does not replace the mandatory annual filing of Form T661 and Schedule 31. When filing Form T661 (Version 26), the claimant ticks Line 212 and enters the Pre-Claim Approval case number on Line 214, reducing the CRA's refundable claim review service standard from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.
