body.text: 6.5 CRA Audit Review Lifecycle, Service Standards, and Dispute Resolution

Once a complete SR&ED claim is filed with the T2 return, the CRA's risk-assessment system either accepts the claim as filed or selects it for technical and financial review. Crucially, once a claim is selected for CRA review, the claimant cannot withdraw the claim.
The 6-Stage CRA Review Process and Service Standards

items: Stage 1 — Initial Contact: The RTA and FR telephone the claimant to explain the review scope, identify selected projects, and schedule a review meeting, followed by a formal letter and document request list.

Stage 2 — Information Requests (30-Day Turnaround): Reviewers request the contemporaneous evidence ticked on Lines 270–282 of Form T661, plus T4 payroll registers, time sheets, trial balances, contracts, and assistance agreements. The claimant is generally given 30 calendar days per request.

Stage 3 — Review Meeting and Project Tour: The RTA and FR interview the actual engineers, scientists, or supervisors who performed the work (conducted virtually via live screen-sharing or demos, or on-site in exceptional cases).

Stage 4 — RTA and FR Findings: The RTA drafts the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report determining which projects or activities pass the "Why" and "How" tests; the FR adjusts qualified expenditures accordingly.

Stage 5 — Proposal Package (30-Day Response Window): The CRA issues a formal Proposal Letter attaching the RTA and FR reports and proposed adjustments. The claimant has 30 calendar days to submit written rebuttals or additional contemporaneous evidence before the file closes.
Stage 6 — Final Assessment / Reassessment and 90-Day Objection Window: The CRA issues the final letter and official Notice of Assessment or Reassessment.

body.text: The CRA's processing service standards (measured in calendar days from receipt of a complete claim and T2 return) are 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed without review; 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review where all projects received Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review where any project lacked Pre-Claim Approval or differed materially from approved work (non-refundable claims do not carry a fixed calendar-day service standard, and the clock pauses whenever delays are caused by the claimant postponing meetings or taking extra time on information requests).

If a disagreement arises during a review, the claimant may escalate through four dispute resolution tiers: first, speaking directly with the assigned RTA and FR; second, escalating to the Research and Technology Manager and Financial Review Manager; third, submitting a request for an administrative review on Form RC532 before the reviewers close the file (within the 30-day proposal window, though Form RC532 does not extend the 90-day objection deadline); and fourth, filing a formal Notice of Objection within 90 calendar days of the date printed on the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, followed if necessary by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
7. Landmark Jurisprudence, Case Law Precedents, and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

Canadian courts have developed a rigorous body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127. Every technical narrative and audit defence strategy in Canada is governed by the Five-Question Judicial Framework established by the Tax Court of Canada in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures known to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty).

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (Ideas consistent with known facts set up to be proved or disproved, rather than mere trial and error).

Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (Objectives and measures set early, planned testing methods, and logical conclusions derived from results).
Did the process result in a technological advancement? (Gaining new knowledge useful beyond the immediate project—including the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis).
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed? (Contemporaneous documentation).

The foundational precedent for all Canadian SR&ED claims; cited in Section 5.6.6 of the CRA Claim Review Manual.

Retrospective reconstructions by outside consultants cannot substitute for direct testimony from the engineers who performed the work.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261)
Reaffirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic 5-question framework is the authoritative legal interpretation of subsection 248(1).
Strict adherence to the scientific method applies across manufacturing and industrial claims.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Allowed 4 process engineering projects despite sparse written records because the witnesses who performed the work gave highly credible oral testimony.
Credible first-hand witness testimony can counter weak paper documentation, as contemporaneous documents are not a strict statutory condition precedent.
Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211
Disallowed the ITC claim where the taxpayer failed to file prescribed Schedule 31 within the 18-month reporting deadline.
All prescribed information must be filed on prescribed forms within the 18-month deadline.
Allowed claims for no-dig underground and industrial pipe rehabilitation technologies, illustrating how an integrated, cross-disciplinary technological project should be evaluated holistically.
Supports grouping interrelated engineering, materials, and mechanical trials into an integrated SR&ED project.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88
Settled that the courts' role is to interpret and elaborate on the statutory meaning of subsection 248(1), and the Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the appropriate interpretation.
Taxpayers cannot argue that CRA administrative guidelines override the judicial 5-question test.
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)

Dismissed appeal on dynamic SQL software claims. Explicitly disagreed that the CRA's 2021 SR&ED Guidelines removed the requirement to follow the scientific method, and upheld the exclusion of an expert report that opined on the ultimate legal question.
Formulating a hypothesis alone is not enough; claimants must prove systematic testing and logical conclusions.
Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18
Allowed claims for tractor design where subsystem integration issues created system uncertainties.
Strong precedent illustrating system uncertainties in manufacturing.
Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 (2023 DTC 1069)

Allowed SR&ED claims for developing antibiotic-free, high-protein, shelf-stable frozen savoury pies. Clarified at para. 89 that "the lacking knowledge must exist in the base of scientific or technological knowledge, not simply be unknown to the claimant".
Demonstrates that unconventional industries (food science) qualify when constraints cannot be met via publicly available knowledge.
Allowed software SR&ED claims for cloud-based SaaS integration and React/Redux performance, finding systemic uncertainty in open-source tool integration beyond routine debugging or optimization.
Encourages holistic evaluation of software projects supported by metrics and testimony.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159
Allowed claims for shelf-stable cold-pressed beverage ("Chrisoda") after initial cans exploded from microbial oxygen release; validated systematic testing via measurable pH and microbial metrics.
Validates observation and quantitative measurement as keys to systematic investigation.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 & Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183

Disallowed claims where prototyping was trial-and-error with vague hypotheses (Vortex Energy) and where narratives were reconstructed and employee wages were split evenly across batches without records (Tuna Temple).
Trial-and-error narratives and evenly split wage estimates without contemporaneous records fail.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173

Split decision: allowed certain 2007–2008 heating element projects, but denied 2006 and 2009 claims and held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports was a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported section 163(2) / section 160 assessments.
Copied technical write-ups can reopen statute-barred years and support gross negligence penalties.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7

Split software/control-systems ruling: Allowed the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control project based on cumulative system uncertainty not resolvable by available methods; Disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 project, holding that modernizing and scaling up with known tools is product development, not experimental development.
Defines the exact boundary in modern software claims: cumulative system-level uncertainty wins, while legacy modernization and scale-up with known tools loses.

body.text: 7.2 Contemporaneous Documentation and Audit Defence Protocol

To survive a joint technical and financial review by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR), claimants must embed documentation into their daily engineering and accounting workflows rather than reconstructing narratives after year-end:

items: Technical Contemporaneous Evidence (Form T661, Lines 270–282): Maintain dated records generated as the work progressed that map directly to the 5 Northwest Hydraulic questions: project planning documents defining the baseline technological limitation and why standard practice failed; explicit records of formulated hypotheses; dated experimental logs, source code commit histories, ticket histories, architecture diagrams, lab notebooks, trial run and scrap records, and quantitative test results; and post-test analytical conclusions.

Financial and Time-Tracking Substantiation: Reconcile all Form T661 expenditure lines to the trial balance, T4 payroll records, and client or grant contracts prior to filing. Replace round-number retrospective percentage estimates (which fail under Ergorecherche and Tuna Temple, 2025 TCC 183) with contemporaneous project time allocations tied to specific people, projects, and hands-on SR&ED tasks. For post-December 15, 2024 capital assets (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and leased equipment (Lines 350/355), maintain purchase invoices, available-for-use dates, lease contracts, and machine operating-hour logbooks proving whether SR&ED usage met the ≥90% ASA threshold or the >50% to <90% SUE and lease primary-use threshold.
